issues.item: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: The threat items imply a trauma context dominated by interpersonal assault or ambush cues (others' sudden movements, ominous silence) rather than toxic chemical exposure. For a chemical exposure trauma, these are hard to reconcile unless there is additional unreported assault/combat context.

issues.item: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal about losing connection to community/culture is not well anchored to the rest of the profile. The other selected items center on intrusive memory, overwhelm, and coping incapacity, but there are no related triggers, memories, or strategies suggesting social/cultural disconnection as a core post-trauma theme.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: This item is the least coherent with the rest of the profile. For a 72-year-old married male Coast Guard patient with toxic chemical exposure, the dominant pattern elsewhere is threat, intrusive sensory memory, and low coping around reminders. 'Lost connection to my community and culture' is not impossible, but it is not well supported by the trauma type or by the other selected threat/memory/appraisal items, which center on danger, overwhelm, and inability to handle recall. It reads as a broader social-identity consequence that is disconnected from the active formulation, where Memory and Threat are tightly linked and Negative Appraisals are threat-focused. This makes that individual appraisal item clinically weakly matched to the rest of the self-report.

vignette: James, a 72-year-old African American Coast Guard veteran, has been struggling with vivid memories and intense reactions since his toxic chemical exposure incident in service. The event occurred during a routine inspection when he was exposed to a highly toxic substance that left him gasping for air and seeing the world through a hazy, terrifying lens. James still remembers the suffocating silence just before the attack, which now triggers an overwhelming sense of danger whenever there is unusual quiet. James’s marriage has been strained as he finds himself on constant guard even within his own home. The slightest sound or sudden absence of noise can trigger intense physical reactions, such as rapid heartbeat and sweating, making it hard for him to relax around his wife, who often notices the tension in his body. His wife tries her best to support him, but James feels that he cannot cope with any form of upset, no matter how slight. He believes that if he allows himself to think about what happened, he will not be able to handle it. One evening as they were watching television together, a moment of silence in the background triggered an intense flashback for James. The memory replayed like a film, and his mind was flooded with photographic images of the toxic exposure. He felt so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to stop whatever he was doing and retreat into himself. These memories often lead him to believe that the world is a dangerous place, reinforcing his sense of threat. The cycle of James’s thoughts and reactions has been self-reinforcing over time. His negative appraisals—such as believing he cannot cope with even the slightest upset or thinking about the event—are deeply intertwined with his heightened sense of threat. For instance, when James hears a sudden silence in the house, it triggers both intense physical reactivity and an overwhelming belief that danger is imminent. This fear makes him more likely to relive the traumatic memories, which then further exacerbate his negative appraisals about his ability to handle distress. James’s daily life has become increasingly challenging as he struggles with these experiences. He avoids going out alone for fear of encountering situations that might trigger his symptoms. His wife reports that James often becomes visibly distressed when they are in quiet environments or when there is unexpected silence, leading him to feel on guard and hyper-vigilant. Recently, James finally decided to seek help after a particularly intense episode where he was overcome with panic at the sound of an empty room while walking through his house. He felt that this continuous state of vigilance and emotional overwhelm had become too much for him to bear alone. James is most afraid of losing control or becoming incapacitated by these memories, but he also hopes that therapy can provide some relief from the constant sense of threat and help him regain a semblance of normalcy in his daily life.
